episodes.label: Episode 1

semantics.summary: Student begins with initial implementation of size() and height() methods, successfully unlocking two new test categories (height and size). This is the starting point of the assignment with basic BST structure already in place.

episodes.outcome: testIsEmpty went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 2

semantics.summary: Student implements isEmpty() method and fixes compilation errors. Continues extending functionality with tree query methods. By end of episode, 5 manual tests passing but containsNonBST() remains unimplemented, causing compilation errors.

episodes.outcome: testContainsNonBST went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 3

semantics.summary: Student implements containsNonBST() method to resolve compilation error. Method compiles but contains logic bug - returns false when should return true. This marks the beginning of a prolonged debugging cycle on the contains functionality.

episodes.outcome: testBasicToString went from passing to failing

episodes.label: Episode 4

semantics.summary: Student attempts first fix to containsNonBST() logic. Same assertion failure persists (expected true, got false). Debugging approach begins with trial-and-error modifications.

episodes.outcome: testBasicToString went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 5

semantics.summary: Student continues debugging containsNonBST() with another iteration. Same test failure remains unchanged, indicating the fix did not address the core issue.

episodes.outcome: testToString went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 6

semantics.summary: Extended debugging period spanning 20+ hours. Student makes multiple attempts to fix containsNonBST() logic across runs 6-8 with no progress. After 6 failed attempts, run 9 achieves breakthrough - containsNonBST() finally passes. Student then pivots to implementing toString() method, which initially causes StackOverflowError due to infinite recursion. Subsequent runs fix the stack overflow and formatting issues. By episode end, toString() fully working and 6 manual tests passing.

episodes.outcome: testPreOrderIterator went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 7

semantics.summary: Student implements tree conversion methods (toArrayList, toArray) and iterator variants (inefficientIterator, preOrderIterator). PreOrderIterator requires 6 debugging runs with evolving error messages (boolean assertions → null values → wrong values → exception handling) before breakthrough at run 25. Student then begins implementing in-order iterator but encounters NullPointerException and logic errors. Extended debugging cycle on in-order iterator spans runs 26-39 with plateau periods. Run 40 achieves breakthrough with in-order iterator finally passing. Episode ends with 10 manual tests passing.

episodes.outcome: testIterator went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 8

semantics.summary: Student expands to automated test suite (BSTTesting). Run 41 shows major breakthrough with 7 new tests passing, unlocking insert category. Insert functionality working for both int and string types with proper return values. Run 42 fixes exception handling for null checks, unlocking edge_cases category. Run 43 introduces compilation error with unreachable code affecting contains tests (11 failures). Run 44 recovers with 13 tests passing after fixing compilation error. Run 45 adds efficiency test (2 new passing) but reveals 3 failing remove tests.

episodes.outcome: testInsertExceptions went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 9

semantics.summary: Student encounters test infrastructure issues. Run 47-48 show test suite collapse to single test with 30 tests disappearing (likely compilation error). Run 49 recovers full test suite but remove tests show new error patterns: testRemove expects true but got false, testRemoveAdvanced expects [1,2,3,15] but got [], testRemoveReturnValue shows NullPointerException.

episodes.outcome: testContainsInts went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 10

semantics.summary: Student debugs remove functionality across extended period. Run 50 achieves breakthrough with 2 new tests passing (testRemove and testRemoveReturnValue), unlocking remove category. However, testRemoveAdvanced still failing with size assertion error (expected 3 but got 2). Runs 51-52 show plateau with no progress on advanced remove case.

episodes.outcome: testRemove went from failing to passing

episodes.label: Episode 11

semantics.summary: Critical regression in remove implementation. Run 53 shows inverted size assertions (expected 4 got 14, expected 3 got 15) in previously passing tests. Run 54 continues with inverted logic and introduces StackOverflowError in testRemoveAdvanced, indicating infinite recursion in remove method.

episodes.outcome: testRemove went from passing to failing

episodes.label: Episode 12

semantics.summary: Student recovers from critical regression. Run 55 achieves breakthrough with all 34 tests passing, including all three previously failing remove tests. The fix resolves both the inverted size tracking logic and the infinite recursion issue in node deletion. This represents successful completion of the entire assignment.

episodes.outcome: testRemove went from failing to passing

semantics.summary: Student verifies stability of the complete implementation. Runs 56-57 confirm all 34 tests continue passing with no changes. Assignment is fully complete with all 14 test categories passing: insert, contains, remove, height, size, isEmpty, toArrayList, toArray, toString, iterator, inefficientIterator, preOrderIterator, edge_cases, and efficiency.

feedback.pattern: Inverted size assertions and pointer-replacement logic errors in remove
feedback.explanation: This test regressed in run 53 after passing in run 50, revealing a critical flaw in the remove implementation's handling of the two-child case. The code diffs show three distinct attempts to fix the successor-finding and node-replacement logic. Run 50's change consolidated the insert and remove paths by making remove return the modified subtree root (root = removeHelper(root, i, b)), which is the correct pattern for BST removal. Run 53 introduced inverted successor logic: the code searched cur.left for the in-order successor (which is incorrect—the successor is the leftmost node in the right subtree), and the size assertions inverted (expected 4 but got 14, expected 3 but got 15), indicating the tree structure was corrupted. Run 54 continued with inverted assertions (expected 14 but got 4), showing the logic remained backwards. Run 55 fixed the core issue by correcting the successor search to use cur.right and traverse left to find the minimum, and properly handling the node replacement with prev tracking and correct subtree linkage. The fix also restored the return-value pattern from removeHelper, ensuring the tree structure remained valid and size tracking stayed accurate. This test and testRemove() share the same underlying bug in the two-child removal case.
nextSteps: Understand the three cases of BST removal: (1) leaf nodes return NULL_NODE to detach, (2) one-child nodes return the non-null child to bypass the current node, (3) two-child nodes find the in-order successor (leftmost node in the right subtree), replace the current node's data with the successor's data, and recursively remove the successor from the right subtree. The key insight is that remove must always return the new root of the subtree to maintain correct parent-child links as the recursion unwinds.

When implementing the two-child case, trace through a concrete example (e.g., removing a node with two children from a tree with 5–7 nodes) to verify that the successor is correctly identified, the data replacement happens, and the recursive call to remove the successor from the right subtree is properly captured and returned. This pattern recurs in EditorTrees Milestone 3 (delete with AVL rebalancing) and Exam 2 (pruneFullSubtreesSize3), where the same pointer-replacement technique detaches subtrees.

Verify that your remove method updates the size counter correctly: size should decrease by exactly 1 when a node is successfully removed, and remain unchanged if the element was not found. Use assertions in your test cases to catch inverted logic early.

feedback.pattern: Sustained in-order iterator logic errors with flag-state management
feedback.explanation: This test took 14 runs to resolve, with 13 consecutive assertion failures after an initial NullPointerException in run 26. The NullPointerException was fixed by run 27, but the iterator logic remained broken: the test expected element 2 but received 1, then null, indicating the traversal order was incorrect or elements were being skipped. The core issue was in the flag-state machine used to track the iterator's position within each node's three-phase traversal (left subtree, current node, right subtree). Run 40's code diff shows a critical fix: the flag logic was revised to properly handle the transition from visiting the left subtree (flag 1) to returning the current node (flag 2) and then visiting the right subtree. The change added logic to check whether the current node being processed is the same as the one being popped from the stack, preventing duplicate processing and ensuring the correct element is returned at each step. The fix also ensured that the right subtree is only pushed back onto the stack if it exists, maintaining the in-order sequence. This pattern recurs in EditorTrees toString() (which requires O(N) in-order traversal) and Exam 3 (which verifies traversal outputs), making precise flag management essential.
nextSteps: Master the iterative in-order traversal pattern using a stack and flag states: (1) push the node with flag 1 (visit left), (2) when popped with flag 1, push the node back with flag 2 (visit self) and push its left child with flag 1, (3) when popped with flag 2, return the node's data and push its right child with flag 1 if it exists. The key is that each node is pushed and popped twice—once to descend left, once to return the data—and the flag distinguishes these phases.

Trace through a small tree (e.g., 3 nodes: 2 as root, 1 as left child, 3 as right child) by hand, writing down the stack contents and flags at each step. Verify that the output is [1, 2, 3] and that no element is skipped or duplicated. This pattern recurs in EditorTrees toString() and Exam 3 mirror constructor verification, where you must predict traversal outputs.

Test your iterator on edge cases: single-node trees, left-skewed trees, right-skewed trees, and balanced trees. Ensure that hasNext() correctly reflects whether elements remain and that next() throws NoSuchElementException when the iterator is exhausted.

feedback.pattern: Infinite recursion in remove leading to StackOverflowError
feedback.explanation: This test failed for 8 runs with 7 assertion failures before hitting a StackOverflowError in run 54, indicating infinite recursion in the remove logic. The assertion failures (runs 45–53) show the tree structure was being corrupted or size tracking was incorrect, similar to testRemoveReturnValue(). The StackOverflowError in run 54 reveals that the recursive removeHelper call was not properly terminating—the return value from the recursive call was not being captured and assigned back to the node's child pointer. Run 55's code diff shows the same fix applied to testRemoveReturnValue(): the successor-finding logic was corrected (right subtree, traverse left), and the node replacement was properly implemented with prev tracking. Critically, the fix ensures that the recursive call to remove the successor is properly returned and assigned, preventing infinite loops. The two-child case now correctly replaces the current node's data with the successor's data, removes the successor from the right subtree, and returns the modified subtree root. This fix resolved both the assertion failures and the infinite recursion.
nextSteps: Ensure that every recursive call to removeHelper captures and returns its result: when removing a node with two children, the call to removeHelper(cur.right, ...) must be assigned back to cur.right (or equivalent), so the tree structure is updated as the recursion unwinds. Missing this assignment causes the tree to become disconnected and can lead to infinite loops if the same node is visited repeatedly.

Verify that your base cases are correct: if the node is NULL_NODE, return NULL_NODE immediately; if the element is found and the node is a leaf, return NULL_NODE; if the element is found and the node has one child, return that child. These base cases ensure the recursion terminates and the tree structure is maintained.

Test your remove method on trees with multiple levels and complex removal sequences (e.g., removing the root, then removing nodes with two children). Use a debugger or print statements to trace the recursion and verify that each removeHelper call returns the correct subtree root.

feedback.pattern: Incorrect containsNonBST() traversal logic returning false when should return true
feedback.explanation: This test failed for 8 runs with 6 consecutive assertion failures, all of the same type: the containsNonBST() method was returning false when it should return true. The test was introduced in run 3 with a compilation error, which was resolved by run 4, but the logic remained incorrect through run 8. Run 9's code diff shows the fix: the containsNonBST() method was implemented to perform a full tree traversal (not a BST search) by checking both left and right subtrees regardless of the comparison result. The key difference from contains() is that containsNonBST() explores the entire tree because the tree structure may not maintain the BST property. The earlier implementations (runs 4–8) used BST-style comparison logic (if target < current, go left; else go right), which would miss elements in the "wrong" subtree. The fix at run 9 ensures all nodes are visited, making the search exhaustive rather than guided by key comparison.
nextSteps: Distinguish between contains() and containsNonBST(): contains() assumes the BST property holds and uses key comparison to prune the search space (left if target < current, right otherwise), while containsNonBST() must visit every node because the tree may not be a valid BST. Implement containsNonBST() as a full tree traversal that checks the current node and recursively searches both subtrees.

When implementing a full tree traversal, use the pattern: if the current node is NULL_NODE, return false; if the current node's data matches the target, return true; otherwise, return the result of searching the left subtree OR the right subtree. This ensures all nodes are examined and the method returns true as soon as a match is found.

Test both methods on the same tree to verify they produce the same result when the tree is a valid BST, and that containsNonBST() finds elements that contains() might miss if the tree is malformed. This pattern recurs in Exam 2 (shortestWordAlongPath), where you navigate the BST using key comparison, showing how the contains pattern generalizes to other tree queries.

feedback.pattern: Sustained pre-order iterator flag-state and stack-management errors
feedback.explanation: This test took 6 runs to resolve, with 6 consecutive assertion failures showing evolving error patterns: first a hasNext() logic error (expected false but got true), then a next() logic error (expected true but got false), then null returns, and finally incorrect element ordering (expected 5 but got 7). These varied errors across runs 19–24 indicate the flag-state machine and stack management were fundamentally misaligned. The pre-order traversal requires visiting nodes in the order: current, left subtree, right subtree—different from in-order (left, current, right). Run 25's code diff shows a significant rewrite: the iterator was refactored to properly initialize the stack with the root node (if it exists) and set the version for concurrent modification detection. The fix also added proper flag-state handling. The key change is that pre-order requires pushing the right child before the left child (so the left child is popped first), and the flag states must correctly distinguish between the initial push (flag 1, process current and push children) and subsequent pops. The version tracking addition was also incorporated.
nextSteps: Master the iterative pre-order traversal pattern: push the root with flag 1; when popped with flag 1, return the node's data immediately, then push the right child (if it exists) with flag 1, then push the left child (if it exists) with flag 1. This ensures nodes are visited in pre-order (current before children) and children are processed in the correct order (left before right, due to stack LIFO behavior).

Trace through a small tree (e.g., 3 nodes: 2 as root, 1 as left child, 3 as right child) by hand, writing down the stack contents at each step. Verify that the output is [2, 1, 3] (pre-order) and that no element is skipped or duplicated. Compare this to in-order [1, 2, 3] to understand how the traversal order changes based on when the current node is visited relative to its children. This pattern recurs in Exam 3 mirror constructor verification and HW6 preOrderInOrderBuild, where you must predict or reconstruct trees from traversal outputs.

Implement version tracking to detect concurrent modifications (e.g., if the tree is modified while the iterator is active). Store the tree's version number when the iterator is created, and throw ConcurrentModificationException if the version changes during iteration. This is a best practice for robust iterators.
